concepts.title: Value vs reference semantics
concepts.summary: Whether passing something to a function copies it or shares it

variants.explain: Go passes structs by value, so `rename` changes its own copy. To change the caller's `u`, take a `*User` and pass `&u`.
The function gets a reference to the same object, so mutating `u.name` is visible to the caller. Reassigning `u` only rebinds the local parameter, so `Cy` never reaches `user`.
The function receives a reference to the same dict, so `u["name"] = "Bo"` changes the caller's object. Rebinding `u` to a new dict only changes the local name.

concepts.title: Nil pointer in an interface
concepts.summary: A Go interface holding a typed nil pointer is not itself `nil`

choices: It panics with a nil dereference
variants.explain: The returned `error` holds a type (`*MyErr`) and a nil value, and an interface is only `nil` when both are unset. Return a literal `nil` on the success path instead of a typed nil pointer.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
var p *int
var x any = p
fmt.Println(p == nil, x == nil)
```
variants.explain: `p` is a nil pointer, but `x` is an interface that now carries the type `*int`, so it doesn't compare equal to `nil`.

concepts.title: Slice aliasing on append
concepts.summary: Go slices can share one backing array, so `append` may overwrite another slice's elements

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
a := []int{1, 2, 3, 4}
b := a[:2]
b = append(b, 99)
fmt.Println(a)
```
variants.explain: `b` has length 2 but capacity 4, so `append` writes into the shared backing array at index 2. It only copies to a new array when capacity runs out.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
s := make([]int, 3, 10)
t := append(s, 1)
u := append(s, 2)
fmt.Println(t[3], u[3])
```
choices: It panics: index out of range
variants.explain: `s` has spare capacity, so both appends write to the same slot of the same backing array; the second overwrites the first. Copy the slice first (or cap it with `s[:3:3]`) if the results must be independent.

concepts.title: Escape analysis
concepts.summary: How the Go compiler decides whether a variable lives on the stack or the heap

variants.q:
Is this safe?

```go
func newCounter() *int {
    n := 0
    return &n
}
```
choices: Yes: the compiler moves `n` to the heap
Only if `n` is created with `new(int)` instead
No: it's a dangling pointer to a dead stack frame
It compiles, but the pointer is `nil` after the function returns
variants.explain: Go's escape analysis moves `n` to the heap because its address leaves the function. Unlike C, returning the address of a local is always safe; it just costs an allocation.

variants.q: You want to see which variables the compiler moved to the heap (output like `moved to heap: n`). Which command shows that?
variants.explain: `-gcflags=-m` prints the compiler's escape and inlining decisions. `gctrace` reports GC cycles and pprof shows where allocations happen at runtime, but neither explains why a value escaped.

concepts.title: Structural typing
concepts.summary: A type fits an interface by having the right shape, not by declaring that it implements it

choices: No: `ID` must declare that it implements `Stringer`
No: only struct types can implement interfaces
Yes: having a `String() string` method is enough
variants.explain: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly: any type with the right method set fits. There is no `implements` keyword.
Types are compared by shape, so an object with extra properties still fits `Point` and (1) compiles. (2) fails only because TypeScript runs an extra excess-property check on fresh object literals.
A `Protocol` is matched by shape, so any class with a compatible `close` method fits. `@runtime_checkable` is only needed for `isinstance` checks at runtime.

concepts.title: Heap profiling
concepts.summary: Finding what allocates memory with a heap profile (pprof, Chrome DevTools)

concepts.title: Switch fallthrough
concepts.summary: Whether a `switch` case runs into the next one when it has no `break`

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
switch x := 1; x {
case 1:
    fmt.Print("a")
case 2:
    fmt.Print("b")
default:
    fmt.Print("c")
}
```
variants.explain: Go cases don't fall through: each case ends on its own unless it says `fallthrough`. In JavaScript the same shape would print all three.
JavaScript cases fall through until a `break` or `return`, so case 1 runs on into case 2 and `default`. The `noFallthroughCasesInSwitch` compiler option flags this.

variants.q:
Python 3.10+. What does this print?

```python
x = 1
match x:
    case 1:
        print("a")
    case 2:
        print("b")
    case _:
        print("c")
```
variants.explain: `match` runs only the first case that matches; there is no fallthrough and no `break` needed. `case _` runs only when nothing above matched.

concepts.title: Deferred call arguments
concepts.summary: A Go `defer` evaluates its arguments right away but runs the call when the function returns

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
x := 1
defer fmt.Println(x)
x = 2
```
choices: Nothing: deferred calls only run on panic
variants.explain: The arguments of a deferred call are evaluated when the `defer` statement runs, so `x` is captured as `1`. Only the call itself waits until the function returns.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
x := 1
defer func() { fmt.Println(x) }()
x = 2
```
variants.explain: The deferred closure takes no arguments, so nothing is captured early; it reads the variable `x` when it runs at return time. Passing `x` as an argument would print `1`.

concepts.title: `finally` and `defer` changing the result
concepts.summary: Cleanup code that runs after `return` can replace the value the caller gets

variants.explain: `finally` runs after the `return 'try'` has been decided, and its own `return` replaces it. A `return` in `finally` also swallows any exception thrown in `try`.

variants.q:
What does `f()` return?

```go
func f() (n int) {
    defer func() { n *= 10 }()
    return 2
}
```
variants.explain: `return 2` assigns `2` to the named result `n`, then deferred functions run and can modify it. Without a named result, the defer couldn't touch the returned value.

variants.q:
What does `f()` return?

```python
def f():
    try:
        return "try"
    finally:
        return "finally"
```
variants.explain: The `finally` block runs after `return "try"` is decided, and its own `return` replaces the value (and would swallow any exception from `try`). Python 3.14 adds a `SyntaxWarning` for this (PEP 765), but it still runs and returns `"finally"`.

concepts.title: Labeled break
concepts.summary: A `break` inside a `switch` or `select` leaves only that statement, not the loop around it

choices: The loop keeps running: `break` only leaves the `select`
The goroutine blocks until `in` is closed too
variants.explain: `break` exits the innermost `for`, `switch` or `select`, here the `select`. Put a label on the loop and use `break loop`, or `return`.

choices: Skips straight to `default` and runs the job
Leaves the `switch`; the loop goes on to the next job
A compile error: `break` in a `switch` needs a label
variants.explain: `break` binds to the nearest `switch`, so the loop carries on. To stop the loop, label it (`outer: for ...`) and use `break outer`.

concepts.title: Map iteration order
concepts.summary: Which order you get when looping over a map or an object's keys

variants.q: You range over the same unchanged `map[string]int` twice in a row. What order do the keys come in?
choices: The order can differ between the two loops
Unspecified, but the same in both loops
variants.explain: Map iteration order is unspecified and the runtime deliberately varies it between loops. `fmt.Println` of a map sorts keys for display, which misleads people into thinking maps are ordered.

variants.q:
What does this log?

```ts
console.log(Object.keys({ b: 1, 2: 1, a: 1, 1: 1 }))
```
variants.explain: Integer-like keys come first in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order. Use a `Map` if you need pure insertion order for every key.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```python
print(list({"b": 1, 2: 1, "a": 1, 1: 1}))
```
choices: An order that can change between runs
variants.explain: Since Python 3.7, dicts keep insertion order for every key, integers included. JavaScript objects differ: they list integer-like keys first. Sets don't keep insertion order.

concepts.title: Closures
concepts.summary: A function that keeps access to the variables of the scope it was created in

variants.explain: Each call to `makeCounter` creates a new `n`, and the returned function keeps its own one alive. `a` has been called three times; `b` has its own counter at 1.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
func makeCounter() func() int {
    n := 0
    return func() int { n++; return n }
}

a := makeCounter()
a(); a()
b := makeCounter()
fmt.Println(a(), b())
```
variants.explain: The closure captures the variable `n` itself, not a copy, and each `makeCounter` call makes a fresh `n`. So `a` reaches 3 while `b` starts again at 1.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```python
def make_counter():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return inc

a = make_counter()
a(); a()
b = make_counter()
print(a(), b())
```
variants.explain: Each `make_counter` call creates a new `n` that its `inc` keeps alive. `nonlocal` lets `inc` rebind it; without it, `n += 1` would raise `UnboundLocalError`.

concepts.title: Loop variable capture in closures
concepts.summary: Whether a closure created in a loop sees one shared variable or a fresh one per iteration

variants.explain: Since Go 1.22 each loop iteration gets its own `i`, so every closure captures a different variable. Before 1.22 the loop shared one `i` and this printed `333`.
`var` is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the same `i`, which is `3` by the time they run. With `let`, each iteration gets its own binding and it logs `0 1 2`.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```python
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])
```
variants.explain: The lambdas look up `i` when they're called, and by then the comprehension's single `i` ended at `2`. Bind it at creation with a default: `lambda i=i: i`.

concepts.title: Lost `this` binding
concepts.summary: A method pulled off its object and called on its own no longer has `this`

choices: A compile error on `const inc = c.inc`
variants.explain: `this` is set by how a function is called, not where it was defined. Called bare, `inc` gets `this === undefined` (class bodies are strict mode), so `this.n` throws.

variants.q: Passing `c.inc` as a callback loses `this`. Which change to `Counter` makes `const inc = c.inc; inc()` increment `c.n`?
choices: Declare it as a field: `inc = () => { this.n++ }`
variants.explain: An arrow function takes `this` from where it's created, which for a class field is the instance. `public` changes nothing at runtime, and `inc.call()` with no argument still passes `undefined`.

concepts.title: Go method values
concepts.summary: Taking `t.Method` as a value binds the receiver at that moment

variants.explain: With a value receiver, `t.Show` copies `t` when the method value is created, so later changes to `t` aren't seen. With a pointer receiver it would print `2`.

choices: It doesn't compile: `t` isn't a pointer
variants.explain: With a pointer receiver, `t.Show` binds `&t`, so the call reads the current `t.n`. Go takes the address of addressable values automatically, so it compiles.

concepts.title: Temporal dead zone
concepts.summary: `let` and `const` exist from the start of their block but throw if used before their line runs

variants.q:
What happens at runtime?

```ts
function show() { console.log(x) }
show()
let x = 1
```
variants.explain: `x` is hoisted but stays uninitialised until `let x = 1` runs, and reading it before then throws. With `var x = 1` it would log `undefined`.

Only `function greet() {}` declarations are usable before their line. A `const` is in its dead zone until assigned; the `TypeError` is what `var greet = ...` would give, since a `var` starts as `undefined`.

concepts.title: Variable shadowing with `:=`
concepts.summary: `:=` in an inner block declares a new variable instead of assigning the outer one

choices: It doesn't compile: `err` is declared twice
variants.explain: Inside the `if`, `:=` declares a new `err` that shadows the outer one, so the outer `err` stays `nil`. Declare `id` first and use `=`, or return inside the block.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
x := 1
if x > 0 {
    x := x + 1
    fmt.Print(x, " ")
}
fmt.Print(x)
```
variants.explain: The inner `x := x + 1` creates a new `x` (initialised from the outer one) that only lives inside the block. The outer `x` is untouched.

concepts.title: Embedding vs inheritance
concepts.summary: Go struct embedding promotes methods but has no virtual dispatch, unlike class inheritance

variants.explain: `Hello` is promoted from `Base` and runs with a `Base` receiver, so it calls `Base.Name`. Embedding is delegation, not overriding; use an interface if behaviour must vary.
Class methods dispatch on the runtime object, so `this.name()` inside `Base.hello` finds `Derived`'s override. Go's struct embedding is the case where this does not happen.
Method lookup on `self` starts at the runtime class, so `Base.hello` finds `Derived.name`. Go's struct embedding is the case where this does not happen.

concepts.title: Method sets
concepts.summary: Whether a value or only a pointer satisfies an interface depends on the method receivers

choices: No: `File` has no methods at all
variants.explain: The method set of `File` excludes pointer-receiver methods, so `File{}` doesn't satisfy `Saver`; `&File{}` does. Auto-addressing applies to direct calls like `f.Save()`, not to interface satisfaction.

variants.q: Now `Save` has a value receiver: `func (f File) Save() error`. Which can be assigned to `var s Saver`?
variants.explain: A pointer's method set includes the value-receiver methods too, so both satisfy the interface. The reverse isn't true: a value doesn't get pointer-receiver methods.

concepts.title: `#private` vs `private`
concepts.summary: TypeScript's `private` is checked only at compile time; `#field` is private at runtime too

variants.explain: `private` is erased when compiling; at runtime `balance` is an ordinary property. The `as any` cast sidesteps the compile-time check, so the value is readable.
`#balance` is a true private field: it isn't a normal property, so no cast or `Object.keys` can see it from outside the class body.

concepts.title: Exported identifiers
concepts.summary: In Go, a lowercase name is private to its package, including to reflection-based encoders

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
type User struct {
    Name  string
    email string
}

b, _ := json.Marshal(User{Name: "Al", email: "a@x.io"})
fmt.Println(string(b))
```
choices: An empty string: `Marshal` returns an error
variants.explain: `encoding/json` only sees exported (capitalised) fields, so `email` is silently skipped. Export it and add a tag like `json:"email"` to control the key.

variants.q: Package `user` defines `type User struct { Name string; email string }`. In package `main`, what does `u.email` give you?
variants.explain: Identifiers starting with a lowercase letter are only visible inside their own package. There's no read-only access; you'd add an exported method like `Email()`.

concepts.title: Pure functions
concepts.summary: Functions whose result depends only on their inputs and that change nothing outside themselves

variants.q: Which of these functions is pure?
variants.explain: Only the last depends on nothing but its arguments and has no side effects. `sort()` mutates its input array, and the others read outside state that can change between calls.

variants.q: Why can `func area(w, h float64) float64 { return w * h }` be cached or run from many goroutines safely, while `func next() int { counter++; return counter }` can't?
choices: `area` takes only value types, which Go copies on each call
`area` depends only on its inputs and changes no shared state
`next` takes no parameters, so there is no key to cache it by
`area` is small enough for the compiler to inline it
variants.explain: Purity is what makes caching and concurrent calls safe: same inputs, same result, no side effects. `next` mutates shared state, so each call depends on the ones before it.

variants.q: Which of these functions is pure?
variants.explain: `sorted` returns a new list and leaves its input alone. `xs.sort()` mutates the caller's list, and the others read or change state outside the function.

concepts.title: Shallow immutability
concepts.summary: `Object.freeze` or a tuple stops changes to the outer object, not to objects nested inside

variants.q:
What does this log?

```ts
const cfg = Object.freeze({ db: { host: 'a' } })
cfg.db.host = 'b'
console.log(cfg.db.host)
```
variants.explain: `freeze` only locks `cfg`'s own properties; `cfg.db` is a separate, unfrozen object. TypeScript's `Readonly` result type is shallow in the same way, so it compiles.

variants.q:
Running as an ES module (strict mode), what happens?

```ts
const list: any = Object.freeze([{ n: 1 }])
list[0].n = 2       // line A
list.push({ n: 3 }) // line B
```
choices: Line A succeeds; line B throws a `TypeError`
Line A throws; line B succeeds
variants.explain: The array itself is frozen, so `push` throws, but the object inside it isn't, so changing `n` works. Deep immutability needs a recursive freeze or immutable data structures.

variants.q:
What does this print?

```python
t = (1, [2])
t[1].append(3)
print(t)
```
choices: A `TypeError`, but the list is changed anyway
variants.explain: A tuple only stops you replacing its items; the list inside is still a mutable object, so `append` works without error. (`t[1] += [3]` is the case that both mutates the list and raises `TypeError`.)

concepts.title: `reduce` without an initial value
concepts.summary: Leaving out `reduce`'s initial value makes the first element the accumulator, and throws on an empty array

variants.q:
What happens?

```ts
const prices: number[] = []
const total = prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p)
```
variants.explain: With no initial value, `reduce` uses the first element as the starting accumulator, and an empty array has none, so it throws. Pass `0` as the second argument.

variants.q:
What does this log?

```ts
const xs = [7]
const r = xs.reduce((a, b) => {
  console.log('called')
  return a + b
})
console.log(r)
```
variants.explain: With one element and no initial value, that element becomes the result and the callback is never called. With an initial value of `0`, the callback would run once.

variants.q:
What happens?

```python
from functools import reduce

total = reduce(lambda a, b: a + b, [])
```
variants.explain: Without an initial value, `reduce` starts from the first item, and an empty list has none. Pass `0` as the third argument, or use `sum`.

concepts.title: Range-over-func iterators
concepts.summary: Go 1.23's `iter.Seq`: a function that calls `yield` for each value can be used in a `for range` loop

choices: It panics with a sentinel the iterator must recover
variants.explain: The loop body is compiled into the `yield` function; `break` makes it return `false`, telling the iterator to stop. The iterator must then return without calling `yield` again.

variants.q: Go 1.23+. An iterator ignores `yield`'s return value and keeps calling it after the loop body did `break`. What happens?
choices: The extra values are silently dropped
The loop body runs again for each extra value
variants.explain: Calling `yield` after it returned `false` is a runtime panic. The compiler can't see this, so iterators must check `yield`'s result.

concepts.title: Generators are lazy
concepts.summary: A generator function's body doesn't run until someone asks for the next value

variants.explain: Calling `gen()` only creates the iterator; the body first runs on `it.next()`. This laziness is why generators can describe infinite or expensive sequences.

choices: It runs out of memory building the sequence
variants.explain: Values are produced one at a time as the loop asks for them, so the infinite loop inside only advances on demand. `break` stops asking and closes the generator.

variants.q:
What is the order of the output?

```python
def gen():
    print("start")
    yield 1

it = gen()
print("created")
next(it)
```
variants.explain: Calling `gen()` only creates the generator object; its body first runs on `next(it)`.

concepts.title: Error wrapping
concepts.summary: Adding context to an error while keeping the original inspectable

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
err := fmt.Errorf("load config: %w", fs.ErrNotExist)
fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist))
```
variants.explain: `%w` wraps the original error, and `errors.Is` walks the wrap chain. With `%v` the original would be flattened into the message and this would print `false`.

variants.q: Given `const err = new Error('load config', { cause: original })`, how do you get `original` back?
choices: You can't: only the message is kept
variants.explain: The `cause` option (ES2022) stores the wrapped error on `err.cause`, so callers can inspect what went wrong underneath.

variants.q:
A caller catches the `RuntimeError` as `err`. Where is the original `FileNotFoundError`?

```python
try:
    open("/missing")
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    raise RuntimeError("load config") from e
```
choices: Nowhere: `from` only changes the traceback text
variants.explain: `raise ... from e` stores the original on `__cause__`, and the traceback shows both. Raising inside `except` without `from` still records it, on `__context__`.

concepts.title: `errors.As`
concepts.summary: Finding an error of a specific type anywhere in a Go wrap chain and getting it as that type

variants.q:
What does this print?

```go
_, err := os.Open("/missing")
err = fmt.Errorf("load: %w", err)

var pe *fs.PathError
if errors.As(err, &pe) {
    fmt.Println(pe.Path)
}
```
choices: `load: open /missing: no such file or directory`
variants.explain: `errors.As` walks the chain, finds the wrapped `*fs.PathError`, and stores it in `pe`. A type assertion `err.(*fs.PathError)` would fail here because it only checks the outer error.

variants.q: Someone writes `errors.As(err, pe)` instead of `errors.As(err, &pe)`, where `pe` is a nil `*fs.PathError`. What happens?
variants.explain: The target parameter is `any`, so it compiles, but `As` needs a pointer to somewhere it can store the match and panics on a nil one. `go vet` catches this.

concepts.title: `errors.Join`
concepts.summary: Go 1.20's way to combine several errors into one that still matches each of them

variants.q:
Go 1.20+. What does this print?

```go
errA := errors.New("a")
errB := errors.New("b")
err := errors.Join(errA, errB)
fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, errB))
```
choices: `false`: only the first error is kept
variants.explain: A joined error exposes all its parts through `Unwrap() []error`, and `errors.Is` and `errors.As` check every one.

variants.q: Go 1.20+. What does `errors.Join(nil, nil) == nil` evaluate to?
choices: `false`: it returns an empty joined error
variants.explain: `Join` drops nil errors and returns `nil` if nothing is left, so you can join results from several steps and still check `err != nil` as usual.

concepts.title: `recover` only covers its own goroutine
concepts.summary: A panic in a goroutine can't be recovered by another goroutine and crashes the whole program

choices: Only the goroutine dies; `main` carries on silently
variants.explain: `recover` only stops a panic in the goroutine whose deferred function calls it. An unrecovered panic in any goroutine terminates the process.

variants.q: An HTTP handler starts `go sendEmail(u)`, and `sendEmail` panics on a nil pointer. `net/http` recovers panics in handlers. What happens?
choices: `net/http` recovers it and logs the stack trace
The request gets a 500, other requests are fine
variants.explain: The server's recovery runs in the handler's goroutine, and `sendEmail` runs in a different one. Background goroutines need their own deferred `recover`.

concepts.title: Unhandled promise rejection
concepts.summary: A rejected promise nobody awaits or catches; since Node 15 it crashes the process by default

variants.q:
On Node 15 or later with default settings, what happens?

```ts
async function sync() {
  throw new Error('db down')
}
sync()
setInterval(tick, 1000)
```
choices: A warning is printed and the interval keeps running
The process exits with the error
variants.explain: The rejected promise is never handled, and since Node 15 `--unhandled-rejections` defaults to `throw`, which crashes the process. Before 15 it only printed a warning.

choices: Yes, as soon as the promise rejects
Yes, but only if `load` throws before its first `await`
Only when the `useUnknownInCatchVariables` option is on
No: the returned promise rejects later, unhandled
variants.explain: An `async` function never throws to its caller; errors, even ones before the first `await`, become a rejected promise. Without `await load()` the `try` has already finished, and the rejection goes unhandled.

concepts.title: Caught values are `unknown`
concepts.summary: JavaScript can throw any value, so TypeScript types the `catch` variable as `unknown`

variants.q: TypeScript 4.4+ with `strict: true`. What is the type of `e` in `try { ... } catch (e) { ... }`?
variants.explain: `strict` turns on `useUnknownInCatchVariables`, so `e` is `unknown` and you have to narrow it (for example `e instanceof Error`) before using `.message`. Without it, `e` is `any`.
A plain string was thrown, and strings have no `message` property. The cast only silences the compiler; that's why `e` is `unknown` and should be checked with `instanceof Error`.

concepts.title: Microtasks vs macrotasks
concepts.summary: Promise callbacks run before timers, once the current synchronous code finishes

variants.q:
What order are these logged in?

```ts
setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'))
console.log('sync')
```
variants.explain: Synchronous code runs first, then the whole microtask queue (promise callbacks), and only then the next macrotask such as a timer. A `0` ms timeout still waits for all microtasks.

variants.q:
What order are these logged in?

```ts
async function f() {
  console.log('a')
  await null
  console.log('b')
}
f()
console.log('c')
```
variants.explain: An `async` function runs synchronously up to its first `await`; the rest is queued as a microtask. So `a` logs, `f` returns, `c` logs, then `b`.

concepts.title: `await` in a loop
concepts.summary: Awaiting each call in turn runs them one after another; starting them all first runs them together

choices: About 100 ms, or less on a multi-core machine
About 20 ms per call, since they share a connection
variants.explain: Each iteration waits for its call before starting the next, so the calls run one after another. `await Promise.all(ids.map(fetchUser))` would start all five at once, at about 100 ms total.

choices: About 500 ms; run each call in its own goroutine
About 100 ms; the HTTP client pipelines the requests
variants.explain: Each call blocks before the next starts, so the time adds up. Running them in goroutines (for example with `errgroup`) lets them wait on the network together; `GOMAXPROCS` doesn't help code that runs one call at a time.

variants.q:
`fetch_user` takes about 100 ms and `ids` has 5 entries. Roughly how long does this take, and what would make it faster?

```python
for user_id in ids:
    await fetch_user(user_id)
```
choices: About 100 ms; `await` already yields to the event loop
About 100 ms, as long as uvloop is installed
About 500 ms; asyncio can't overlap I/O, so use threads
variants.explain: Each `await` waits for its call to finish before the loop moves on. Yielding to the event loop lets other tasks run, but this loop has nothing else started; `gather` would take about 100 ms.

concepts.title: Async callbacks in `forEach` and `map`
concepts.summary: Passing an `async` function to `forEach` or `map` gives back promises nobody waits for

variants.q:
`save` takes 50 ms. When is `done` logged?

```ts
ids.forEach(async (id) => {
  await save(id)
})
console.log('done')
```
choices: Right away, before the saves finish
variants.explain: `forEach` calls each callback and ignores the promise it returns, so nothing waits. Use `for...of` with `await`, or `await Promise.all(ids.map(save))`.

variants.q:
`load` returns `Promise<User>`. What is the type of `users`?

```ts
const users = ids.map(async (id) => load(id))
```
variants.explain: `map` returns whatever the callback returns, and an `async` callback always returns a promise. Wrap it in `await Promise.all(...)` to get a `User[]`.

variants.q:
`load` is an `async def` function. After this line, what is `results`?

```python
results = [load(i) for i in ids]
```
choices: A list of strings; each call ran in order
A list of tasks already running in the background
A list of coroutine objects; no `load` body has run yet
variants.explain: Calling an `async def` function only creates a coroutine; nothing runs until it's awaited or wrapped in a task. Use `await asyncio.gather(*(load(i) for i in ids))`.

concepts.title: Cooperative cancellation
concepts.summary: Cancelling a `context` or an `AbortSignal` only sends a signal; work stops only if it checks

choices: The goroutine panics with `context deadline exceeded`
The goroutine keeps going until it finishes all rows
`process` returns early on its next call
variants.explain: Cancelling closes `ctx.Done()`, nothing more; Go has no way to kill a goroutine from outside. The loop has to check `ctx.Err()` or `ctx.Done()` to stop.

variants.q:
`processAll` loops over `rows` and never looks at `signal`. What happens after 1 s?

```ts
const ac = new AbortController()
setTimeout(() => ac.abort(), 1000)
await processAll(rows, ac.signal)
```
choices: The loop keeps going until it finishes
The event loop drops the remaining work
variants.explain: `abort()` only flips `signal.aborted` and fires an `abort` event. APIs like `fetch` react to it, but your own code has to check the signal or pass it on.

concepts.title: errgroup
concepts.summary: Running goroutines together and collecting the first error, optionally cancelling the rest

variants.q: Several functions started with `g.Go` on an `errgroup.Group` return errors. What does `g.Wait()` return?
choices: The error from the function started first
variants.explain: `Wait` blocks until every function has returned, then returns the first non-nil error. The others are dropped.

variants.q: After `g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(parent)`, when is `ctx` cancelled (assuming `parent` isn't)?
choices: On the first non-nil error, or when `Wait` returns
Never: you have to call a cancel function yourself
Only once every `g.Go` function has returned an error
As soon as any `g.Go` function returns, error or not
variants.explain: The derived context is cancelled on the first error (or when `Wait` returns), so the other goroutines can stop early by watching `ctx`.

concepts.title: Promise.allSettled
concepts.summary: Waiting for every promise to finish and getting each outcome, even when some reject

variants.q: What happens with `await Promise.allSettled([p1, p2])` if `p1` rejects?
choices: It rejects at once with `p1`'s reason
It resolves with only `p2`'s value in the array
It waits for both, then resolves with a status per promise
variants.explain: `allSettled` never rejects. It waits for every promise and reports each one's outcome; `Promise.all` is the one that rejects on the first failure.

variants.q:
What does this log?

```ts
const results = await Promise.allSettled([
  Promise.resolve(1),
  Promise.reject(new Error('x')),
])
console.log(results.map((r) => r.status))
```
variants.explain: Each result has `status: 'fulfilled'` with a `value`, or `status: 'rejected'` with a `reason`.

concepts.title: Data race
concepts.summary: Unsynchronised concurrent access to the same memory where at least one access is a write

variants.q: Which of these is a data race?
choices: Two threads read the same variable at once, with no lock
Two tasks finish in a different order on each run
One thread writes a variable while another reads it, unsynchronised
Two threads each wait for a lock the other holds
variants.explain: A data race needs concurrent access, at least one write, and no synchronisation. Concurrent reads alone are safe, tasks finishing in varying order is a (possibly harmless) race condition, and waiting on each other's locks is a deadlock.

variants.q: Two threads run `count++` on a shared counter with no lock. Why can increments be lost?
choices: The compiler drops one increment as redundant
CPU caches never write the value back to memory
Both threads can read the old value before either writes
The counter overflows when both add at once
variants.explain: `count++` is a read, an add and a write, so both threads can read the same old value and write back the same result, losing one increment. A lock or an atomic increment fixes it; in Go, `go test -race` detects it.

concepts.title: Deadlock
concepts.summary: Two or more parties each waiting for the other, so none can proceed

variants.q:
What happens?

```go
func main() {
    ch := make(chan int)
    ch <- 1
    fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
```
choices: It crashes: `all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!`
variants.explain: A send on an unbuffered channel blocks until another goroutine receives, and there is none. The runtime sees every goroutine blocked and aborts. `make(chan int, 1)` would let it print `1`.

variants.q: Worker 1 locks account A then account B; worker 2 locks B then A. Under load they sometimes hang forever. What's the standard fix?
choices: Take the locks in one global order (e.g. by account id)
Add a short sleep between taking the two locks
Use a read-write lock instead of a mutex
Hold each lock for a shorter time
variants.explain: Each worker holds one lock and waits for the other's: a lock-ordering deadlock. A consistent order removes the cycle; sleeps only make it rarer.

concepts.title: Goroutine leak
concepts.summary: A goroutine blocked forever on a channel nobody will use again, never freed

choices: The garbage collector frees it once `ch` is unreachable
It panics: send on closed channel
variants.explain: Nobody will ever receive from `ch`, so the send blocks forever. Blocked goroutines are never garbage collected, so each timeout leaks one.

variants.q: In the same `fetch` function, which one-line change stops the leak?
variants.explain: With a buffer of one, the send always succeeds and the goroutine exits even if nobody reads. Closing `ch` from `fetch` would make the late send panic.

concepts.title: Copying a mutex
concepts.summary: A copied `sync.Mutex` is a separate lock, so it protects nothing

variants.explain: The value receiver copies the whole struct, lock and counter included, on every call, so each call increments its own copy. Use `func (c *Counter) Inc()`.

variants.q: `go vet` reports `passes lock by value: Stats contains sync.Mutex` for `func report(s Stats)`. Why is that a bug?
choices: Copying a mutex is slow, so it costs time on every call
The copy is a separate lock, so it doesn't exclude users of the original
A copied mutex always starts locked, so `report` deadlocks
A `sync.Mutex` can't be passed to a function at all
variants.explain: A copy is an independent lock, so holding it doesn't stop others touching the original data, and if it was copied while locked it stays locked. Pass `*Stats`.

concepts.title: Bounded concurrency
concepts.summary: Limiting how many tasks run at once, with a semaphore channel or `errgroup.SetLimit`

choices: Runs the fetches in batches of 3, waiting for each batch to finish
Retries each fetch up to 3 times
Keeps at most 3 fetches running at any time
Starts all fetches, but only 3 results are kept
variants.explain: The buffered channel is a semaphore: the loop blocks on the send when 3 slots are taken and continues as soon as any fetch frees one. It is a sliding window, not fixed batches.

variants.q: After `g.SetLimit(3)` on an `errgroup.Group`, what does the 4th call to `g.Go` do while 3 functions are still running?
choices: Blocks until one of the running functions returns
Starts anyway; the limit only applies to `Wait`
variants.explain: `Go` blocks until a slot is free, so the loop calling it is throttled. `TryGo` is the variant that returns `false` instead of blocking.

variants.q:
What does the semaphore do here?

```python
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(3)

async def fetch_one(url):
    async with sem:
        return await fetch(url)

await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_one(u) for u in urls))
```
choices: Runs the fetches in batches of 3, waiting for each batch
Retries each fetch up to 3 times
Keeps at most 3 fetches running at any time
variants.explain: Every coroutine starts, but only 3 can hold the semaphore at once; the next one enters as soon as any fetch releases it. It's a sliding window, not fixed batches.

concepts.title: Blocking the event loop
concepts.summary: CPU-heavy synchronous code in Node stops every other request until it finishes

variants.q: One Node HTTP handler runs a synchronous loop that takes 2 s. Another request arrives during that time. What happens to it?
choices: Node runs it on another thread
It waits until the loop finishes
It runs interleaved with the loop
variants.explain: JavaScript runs on one thread per event loop, and synchronous code can't be interrupted. Move CPU-heavy work to `worker_threads` or another process.

variants.q:
Does this stop `heavyHash()` (a 2 s CPU loop) from blocking other requests?

```ts
const h = await new Promise((resolve) => resolve(heavyHash()))
```
choices: Yes: promises run on a background thread
Yes, as long as the handler is `async`
variants.explain: The function passed to `new Promise` runs immediately, on the main thread. Promises schedule when callbacks run; they don't move work off the thread.

variants.q:
In an asyncio web server, one handler does this. What happens to other requests during those 2 seconds?

```python
async def handler(request):
    time.sleep(2)
    return "ok"
```
choices: They run normally, since the handler is `async`
They wait until the sleep ends
asyncio moves them to another thread
asyncio raises a `RuntimeError` for the blocking call
variants.explain: `time.sleep` blocks the event loop's only thread, so nothing else runs. Use `await asyncio.sleep(2)`, or `asyncio.to_thread` for blocking or CPU-heavy work.
